newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German jobless rise casts doubt on recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German jobless rise casts doubt on recovery.

text.p: Germany's unemployment has spilled over the four million mark, raising fresh doubts about its economic recovery just as Bonn struggles to squeeze its 1997 budget into Maastricht's tight corset.

Figures released on Thursday showed unemployment rose to a seasonally adjusted 4.04 million in October, the first time it passed that mark since German unification in 1990. That brought the overall jobless rate up to 10.6 percent.

The gloomy numbers emerged soon after Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he was still three billion marks ($1.99 billion) short of funds for his 1997 budget and would probably have to cut the Federal Labour Office budget by another one billion.
The Defence Ministry added to his problems by saying it may need up to two billion marks more than planned next year to pay old bills and finance Germany's troop presence in Bosnia.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition nearly collapsed this week amid disputes over how to plug the budget hole without overstepping the Maastricht requirement to keep new borrowing down to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
But Waigel said he was confident that Kohl's coalition, which has since papered over some of its cracks, would find ways in the next few days of cutting spending even further.
"We in the federal government, and I assume the federal states will follow, are doing all possible to meet the deficit criterion of below three percent for 1997 in Germany," he told German Radio.

The jobless figures showed an unexpectedly strong jump of 41,000 from September. The 10.6 percent rate, up from 10.4 in September, broke down into 9.4 percent (2.89 million people) in west Germany and 15.5 percent (1.15 million) in east Germany.

Waigel said mounting joblessness meant Bonn had to pay out an extra 13 billion marks in unemployment and other benefits this year. "This cannot happen again next year -- we cannot afford it," he said.

The rise in unemployment was stronger than independent economists had been expecting. The Labour Office said the rise could be stopped, but dampened hopes that high unemployment levels would begin to come down any time soon.

"Economic growth is not yet strong enough and based on our estimates and estimates from the government we expect average pan-German unemployment to be around 3.95 million in 1996 and 1997," said Klaus Leven, labour office vice-president.

Economists said the third strong rise in unemployment in as many months raised fresh doubts about the country's slow recovery and the government's chances of reining in its budget to qualify for European monetary union.
"The present moderate economic upturn cannot create new jobs. We have too slow a recovery, and higher demand is satisfied by overtime," said Christian Sobotta of LGT Asset Mangement in Frankfurt.
"The likelihood of a sustained, strong bounce in activity is clearly becoming more remote," Robert Prior-Wandesforde, a James Capel economist in London, said.
Earlier this week, the Federation of German Chambers of Commerce forecast economic growth of 1.5 to two percent in 1997, less than the government's 2.5 percent projection.
Waigel at least had one victory on Thursday when the lower house of parliament passed a diluted 1997 tax bill.

His 1997 deficit target is 56.6 billion marks -- equivalent to 2.5 percent of forecast GDP -- but the exact amount of savings needed to meet this will only become clear when new tax revenue estimates are published on Friday.
Economists said the shortfall could be up to five billion.
In the midst of all this, Waigel also took the time to criticise former chancellor Helmut Schmidt for a stinging attack he made on Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.
Waigel said Schmidt, who published the broadside in his weekly newspaper Die Zeit, was wrong to call for a more flexible interpretation of the strict Maastricht criteria. ($1=1.5087 Mark)
